Abrogated
ăb´rō-gā-tĕd
v. (repealed, annulled by authority; used of the ceremonial law under the new covenant)
Latin abrogare, to repeal a law by the vote of the people — ab, away, and rogare, to propose a law. A law abrogated is not broken but withdrawn by the authority that gave it.

Biblical Definition

To be abrogated is to be repealed by the lawgiver. Hebrews says of the priestly commandment, “there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof” (Heb 7:18), and of the first covenant, “in that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away” (Heb 8:13). Paul: Christ has abolished “in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances” (Eph 2:15), “blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us… nailing it to his cross” (Col 2:14). The moral law is not among them: “Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law” (Rom 3:31).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines abrogate as to repeal; to annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or his successor.

expand to see more

ABROGATE, v.t. To repeal; to annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or his successor; applied to the repeal of laws, decrees, ordinances, the abolition of established customs, &c.

Key Scripture

Heb 7:18 — "For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof."

Heb 8:13 — "In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away."

Eph 2:15 — "Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;"

Col 2:14 — "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;"

Rom 3:31 — "Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law."

Modern Corruption

The whole law is declared abrogated or none of it is, and the Confession distinguishes the ceremonial, the judicial and the moral.

expand to see more

Everything turns on what was repealed. The Reformed division is threefold: the ceremonial law, which pointed forward and is abrogated in Christ; the judicial law given to Israel as a body politic, which expired with that state, though its general equity may still instruct a magistrate; and the moral law, summarised in the ten commandments, which the Confession says doth for ever bind all, justified persons as well as others. Romans 3:31 is the hinge: do we make void the law through faith? God forbid; yea, we establish the law. Faith does not repeal the standard; it satisfies it in Christ and then writes it on the heart.

The antinomian collapse takes Colossians 2:14 to have nailed the whole law to the cross, and reads any appeal to a commandment as a return to bondage. But the handwriting of ordinances that was against us is a debt-note, not a moral standard, and Paul who wrote it also told children to honour father and mother because it is the first commandment with promise. The Judaising collapse runs the other way, reinstating what Hebrews says is ready to vanish away — feasts, food laws, a priesthood, a temple — and Galatians is the letter written against it.

Hebrews 8:13 has a note of tenderness that is easy to miss. That which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away: the old covenant is described as an aged thing near its end, not as an enemy destroyed. It served, it pointed, and it is honoured in its passing. Christians who speak of the Old Testament with contempt have misread the tone as well as the doctrine, and Hebrews spends its whole length proving the new by the reverent exposition of the old.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek athetesis (G115), a setting aside, disannulling; katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative, abolish; exaleipho (G1813), to blot out; palaioo (G3822), to make or become old.

expand to see more

Greek athetesis (G115) — disannulling, putting away; Hebrews 7:18, 9:26.

Greek katargeo (G2673) — to abolish, make of none effect; Ephesians 2:15, 2 Timothy 1:10, 2 Corinthians 3:13.

Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to blot out; Colossians 2:14, Acts 3:19; palaioo (G3822), Hebrews 8:13.

Usage

"“A disannulling of the commandment going before” — repealed by the Lawgiver, not broken."

"“Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us” — a debt-note, not a standard."

"“Yea, we establish the law” — the hinge the antinomian must get past."
